title: IMAGEBIND: One Embedding Space To Bind Them All
problem: Learning a true joint embedding across many modalities is infeasible with existing approaches because they require acquiring all types and combinations of paired data with the same set of images.

Existing multimodal methods use only a single pair of modalities or a few visual modalities, so the final embeddings are limited to the modality pairs seen during training and cannot transfer directly across other modality pairs.
Unlocking zero-shot classification for non-image modalities normally requires paired text data for each modality.

limitations: [6] Our embeddings are trained without a specific downstream task, and thus lag the performance of specialist models.
[6] Our model is a research prototype and cannot be readily used for real world applications ( Appendix F).
[F] IMAGEBIND leverages the image-text embeddings learned by a pretrained model on large web-based data which has biases as documented in different studies [60].
[F] These joint embeddings are thus limited to the concepts present in the datasets.
[F] For example, the thermal datasets we used are limited to outdoor street scenes, while the depth datasets are limited to indoor scenes.
contributions: [1] We present IMAGEBIND, which learns a single shared representation space by leveraging multiple types of image-paired data. It does not need datasets where all modalities co-occur with each other. Instead, we leverage the binding property of images and we show that just aligning each modality's embedding to image embeddings leads to an emergent alignment across all of the modalities. IMAGEBIND can be initialized with large-scale vision-language models such as CLIP [60], thereby leveraging the rich image and text representations of these models. We use large-scale image-text paired data along with naturally paired 'self-supervised' data across four new modalities - audio, depth, thermal, and Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) readings - and show strong emergent zero-shot classification and retrieval performance on tasks for each of these modalities. Finally, we show that IMAGEBIND's joint embeddings can be used for a wide variety of compositional tasks, including cross-modal retrieval, combining embeddings via arithmetic, detecting audio sources in images, and generating images given audio input.
